summary: Specifies TLS cipher suites that use the Camellia block cipher, adding versions that use newer SHA-2 hash algorithms alongside those in RFC 4132. It is a Proposed Standard and replaced RFC 4132.

eli5.summary: Camellia is a secret-scrambling recipe. This lets secure web connections use it with newer stamps for checking messages weren't changed.

questions: which tls versions can use sha256 camellia cipher suites
subtitle: TLS cipher suites that use the Camellia block cipher, now with SHA-256 variants alongside the SHA-1 ones.

tldr.problem: TLS needs named cipher suites before a client and server can use the Camellia block cipher. RFC 4132 defined those suites only with SHA-1 based message authentication.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5932 keeps the SHA-1 suites and adds counterparts that use SHA-256 for the MAC and the TLS 1.2 pseudorandom function. Each suite pairs Camellia in CBC mode with a 128-bit or 256-bit key and one of six key exchange methods.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5932 obsoletes RFC 4132 and has been updated by RFC 10015. The new SHA-256 suites MUST NOT be negotiated by TLS 1.1 or earlier.

today: RFC 5932 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2010. It obsoletes RFC 4132 and has been updated by RFC 10015; it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 5932 adds cipher suites to the Transport Layer Security protocol (TLS 1.2, RFC 5246) so that it can use the Camellia block cipher, which RFC 3713 describes. It builds on the suites originally specified in RFC 4132 by adding variants that use the SHA-2 family of hash algorithms.

The document obsoletes RFC 4132. It contains no new protocol machinery: it assigns names and numbers to cipher suites and says how each part of a suite is to be computed.
sections.eli5: TLS keeps a menu of ways to scramble messages. This document adds more Camellia dishes to the menu.

sections.title: The Cipher Suites
sections.content:
There are 24 suites in four groups of six. Each group has one entry for each key exchange: RSA, DH_DSS, DH_RSA, DHE_DSS, DHE_RSA and DH_anon. The groups are Camellia with a 128-bit key and SHA, Camellia with a 256-bit key and SHA, and the same two with SHA256.

Each suite has a two-byte identifier. For example, TLS_RSA_WITH_CAMELLIA_128_CBC_SHA is { 0x00,0x41 } and TLS_RSA_WITH_CAMELLIA_128_CBC_SHA256 is { 0x00,0xBA }. The 128-bit SHA group runs from 0x41 to 0x46, the 256-bit SHA group from 0x84 to 0x89, the 128-bit SHA256 group from 0xBA to 0xBF and the 256-bit SHA256 group from 0xC0 to 0xC5.
sections.eli5: Each cipher suite is a combo meal with a code number: which way to swap secrets, which scrambler, and which seal to check the message.

sections.title: How the Suites Are Built
sections.content:
The key exchanges (RSA, DHE_RSA, DH_RSA, DHE_DSS, DH_DSS and DH_anon) work exactly as RFC 5246 defines them. The cipher is Camellia in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode. The CAMELLIA_128_CBC suites use a 128-bit key and a 128-bit IV, and the CAMELLIA_256_CBC suites use a 256-bit key and a 128-bit IV.

Suites ending in _SHA use HMAC-SHA1 as the MAC algorithm. With TLS versions before 1.2, the pseudorandom function (PRF) is computed as that version of TLS specifies.

Suites ending in _SHA256 use HMAC-SHA-256 as the MAC, and the PRF is the TLS PRF from RFC 5246 with SHA-256 as the hash. Because of this, they MUST NOT be negotiated by TLS 1.1 or earlier. A client MUST NOT offer them unless it also offers TLS 1.2 or later, and a server that selects an earlier version MUST NOT select one of them.
sections.eli5: The scrambler uses a secret key. The SHA seal is like wax on an envelope, and the newer SHA-256 wax is only allowed with the newest version of TLS.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA updated the registry entries for the twelve SHA suites that RFC 4132 had allocated (0x41 to 0x46 and 0x84 to 0x89) so that they reference this document instead. It also allocated twelve new numbers in the TLS Cipher Suite Registry for the SHA256 suites (0xBA to 0xBF and 0xC0 to 0xC5).
sections.eli5: A librarian keeps the official list of code numbers. The old numbers now point to this document, and twelve new numbers were added.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says that when it was written there were no known weak keys for Camellia and no security problem had been found in it, citing the NESSIE project, CRYPTREC and a paper on impossible differential cryptanalysis of reduced-round Camellia-128. That is a statement about the time of writing, not a lasting guarantee.

It also points to the security discussion throughout RFC 5246, especially its Appendices D, E and F. It adds no other security analysis of its own.
sections.eli5: When this was written, nobody had found a way to break Camellia. It also tells readers to look at the TLS rules for more safety advice.
